findings.breaking_input: Deal with `--rival stitch` where the receipt is DRAFTED and `docs/design/explore/<id>/rival-stitch/index.html` exists, but `.claude/state/design/renders/<id>--rival-stitch/` has a meta whose `viewport` is `1440x900@2` while the deal's `--viewport` is `1440x900` (or has no meta at all because `design-explore.sh rival` ran the adapter, the adapter exited 0, and the renderer then refused/never ran so nothing was recorded).
findings.why: The fix named for L1 was not applied: `latestRender` is the same function and still ends `if (!best) fail(...)` only when a best exists at some point; the `viewport !== \`${viewport}@1\`` filter skips every meta whose viewport is a later iteration, and when no meta matches at all the function falls through to `return { file, sha: best.m.screenshot_sha256 }` with `best` still null → `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'm')`. The check at line 129 is against `${viewport}@1` (an `@1` iteration marker) while the metas the tests write carry `"viewport": "1440x900@1"` only for iter 0; an explore re-rendered once carries `1440x900@2` and the whole deal crashes with a stack trace and code 1, the same exit code as a bash syntax error. Rivals make this reachable: the adapter DRAFTED and the render are two separate processes, so `receipt.status === DRAFTED` with no render is a normal state after `rival` exits non-zero.
findings.fix:
Have `latestRender` call `fail(`rival-

has no render at ${viewport}; render it again`)` when `best` is null or when no meta matches the requested viewport, and never return an object whose fields came from a null `best`.
findings.twin_of: A caller read the parser's "someone else" code, 1, which is also bash's crash code -> a verdict gets a code the runtime never produces by accident; every unknown code is judged.

findings.breaking_input: Two metas in `.claude/state/design/renders/jx--rival-stitch/` both with `iter: 0`, `viewport: "1440x900@1"` and the SAME `screenshot_sha256` but different `route` values — the tie test only fires when `best.m.screenshot_sha256 !== m.screenshot_sha256`. With identical pixels (the determinism check deliberately produces them: the S3 evidence shows sessions `p07-s3c`/`p07-s3d` refused as 'identical pixels already recorded' — identical hashes), no failure fires and `best` stays as whichever meta `readdirSync` returned first. The item's declared `sha256` and the copied file are then a function of directory order, not the explore.
findings.why: The check added for L2 (`if (best && best.iter === iter && best.m.screenshot_sha256 !== m.screenshot_sha256) fail(...)`) is keyed on the render bytes being different. Two renders of the same page, at one iter, is exactly the duplicate the L2 attack was about, and the guard is silent on it: the deal binds the item to one of two screens and the jury's `key.json` gets a hash another valid run would not produce. The pattern is the L2 twin: settle a tie by whatever the filesystem returned first.
findings.fix: Count metas at the maximum iter regardless of hash: `if (best && best.iter === iter) fail(...)` (or group by iter and require exactly one); compare by route and hash only to improve the message.
findings.twin_of: A tie settled by directory order -> exactly one at the max, or refuse

findings.breaking_input: `design-explore.sh rival jx` succeeds; `design-jury jury jx --n 5 --seed 7 --rival stitch <refs>` deals; a juror ranks; `jury-check` writes `result.json` with `valid` true for each ranking. Then the explore directory is regenerated (or the rival dir is `rm -rf`'d and re-drafted) and the SAME `key.json` is used to score, but `result.json` on disk is from the previous deal: its `res.id === key.id` and `res.n === key.n` still match (same explore, same N), `Date.parse(res.checked) >= Date.parse(key.dealt)` still holds if the clock moved forward, and `r.ranked.every((x) => allLabels.has(x))` passes because the label set is the same `item-a..item-e` — but the LABELS map to different items in the new deal. The rival rate is computed against the new key's `rivLabels`/`arcLabels` while the ranking's labels point at the previous deal's items.
findings.why: The fix for L5 validates id, n and a check time — all of which survive a re-deal of the same explore with the same N. The one thing that would bind the rankings to the deal is the item-to-label mapping (the key's `items[].sha256` or the deal's `dealt` time against the ranking's `mtime`), and `unblind` never checks either. The sealed prediction is receipted off the wrong rankings with `res.checked` after `key.dealt` — the L5 rule was tightened but the binding it needed (the content the label names) was not added, so the 'rate read from a record not bound to the deal' pattern survives the fix.
findings.fix: In `unblind`, require the key to carry the deal's exact item hashes and require `result.json` to name that key (a `key_sha256` of the sealed key, or `dealt` equality), refusing a `result.json` whose provenance is another deal; or refuse any `result.json` written before the current `key.json`'s mtime.
findings.twin_of: A rate read from a record not bound to the deal -> the record must carry this deal id, n, a check time after the deal, and only its labels

findings.breaking_input: The adapter writes `docs/design/explore/<runId>/rival-<provider>` after `lstat`ing each of `[ROOT/docs, docs/design, exploreRoot, exploreDir, rivalDir]` for a symlink. But `design-explore.sh rival` takes `ID` from `argv[1]` and `$EX=$ROOT/docs/design/explore/$ID`; the shell case is `[ -d "$EX" ]`. A `--variant`-style ID is validated by the script's id grammar, but `design-explore.sh` passes `$ID` to the adapter as `--run`, and the adapter's `id()` allows 64 lowercase chars with hyphens; the script's own ID grammar is separate. If a `docs/design/explore/<id>/rival-stitch` junction can be planted (a Windows directory junction is `lstat`-invisible on some filesystems, and the fix only lstat-checks the components it constructs, not that the resolved realpath stays under `exploreRoot`), `renameSync(stage, rivalDir)` lands outside the explore.
findings.why: The fix for B5 was listed as applied ('lstat every component and refuse a link; stage under the run own state and rename only on success') but the diff only lstat-checks the components in the literal chain from `ROOT`; it never compares `realpathSync(rivalDir)` to `realpathSync(exploreRoot)`. On Windows a junction (`mklink /J`) is reported by `lstat` as a directory on several Node versions, and `rmSync(..., {recursive:true, force:true})` follows it. The check added for one entry point (the direct chain) was not applied to the resolved path, so the write is not contained to the explore.
findings.fix: After constructing `rivalDir`, `realpathSync(dirname(rivalDir))` and require it to start with `realpathSync(exploreRoot) + sep`; use `lstat` on the final component and `stat` on the parent, and refuse if either is a reparse point.
findings.twin_of: A path from a metadata file trusted because it had no `..` -> a file read on a record's word is realpath-contained to the directory it was found through, a regular file, and the type it claims

findings.breaking_input: A rival whose receipt says `"sdk":"@google/stitch-sdk@0.3.5"` but whose `vendored.page_sha256` was computed over a page whose bytes were produced by a namespace other than `@google/stitch-sdk` — the receipt is trusted as the record of *which SDK* drafted, and the code only binds `rec.sdk`'s version. The version regex `/^(@?[a-z0-9][a-z0-9._/-]*)@([0-9][0-9A-Za-z.+-]{0,40})$/` accepts `@arc/evil@0.0.1` and any local package name; nothing in the deal checks that `pkg` equals `PROVIDERS[pname].pkg` (the pinned package for that provider). `design-rival.mjs` writes `sdk: provider.pkg` so the production path is fine, but the deal trusts the receipt file as the source of truth for the version stamp — a hand-edited or copied receipt from another provider's run yields a `provenance` that Phase 08 will accept as a Stitch draft.
findings.why: The blocker that Phase 08 refuses on is the version stamp, and the deal reads it from a JSON file under `state/` that this run may not have written. The fix for L3 checked for a version; it did not check that the version belongs to the provider the deal names. A receipt can name any package with any version, so the 'provenance comes from the adapter receipt, never from the dir name' claim is true only if the receipt itself is bound to the adapter run — and it is not.
findings.fix: At deal time, compare `rec.sdk` against `PROVIDERS[pname].pkg` for the requested provider and `rec.provider` against `pname`; refuse a receipt whose package is not the pinned one.
findings.twin_of: The licence was checked on one input and the fetch made on another -> every permission check binds to the exact value that is then used

findings.breaking_input: A brief whose `sources.md` has a provenance row `| img-01.png | unused | license text |` in a table that is NOT the reference-pack table (e.g. a licensing table listing every asset the brief consulted), and the same `img-01.png` placed into `refpacks/` by a separate mechanism. Or a `sources.md` with a line `| img-01.png-extra |` — `rows` is built from the whole file and `.includes(full)` finds the basename inside a longer cell.
findings.why: The reference provenance check was reported fixed in the earlier round (L4 said 'split each row into cells, require cells[0].trim() === full'), but the code here still splits the row on `|`, trims each cell and asks `.includes(full)`. `includes` finds the filename anywhere in the row — any column, inside a longer value — and the rows string is built from the whole file, so an unrelated table that mentions the basename admits the image. The reference binding promised by the fix is the L4 twin pattern (an allow-branch that must name the exact pair it admits) and it is still an `includes`.
findings.fix: Split each `|` row into its cells, require the cell that names the reference to equal `full` exactly (after trimming), require exactly one such row, and refuse on zero or on more than one; do not search the whole file as one string.
findings.twin_of: An allow-branch names the exact pair it admits; every other value, empty included, takes the refusal

findings.breaking_input: A provider answer whose `htmlUrl` is on `contribution.usercontent.google.com` but is `https://contribution.usercontent.google.com/d?x=%2e%2e%2fsecret` or a percent-encoded path that resolves to a different resource on the same host; `readAnswer` checks protocol, userinfo, hostname, port and (for the answer's own screen) that `htmlUrl` equals `screen.htmlCode.downloadUrl`. But `download()` then fetches that URL and accepts a 200 with any `content-type`. The screen's own `downloadUrl` can be `https://contribution.usercontent.google.com/anything` — nothing binds the URL's path to the `download` prefix observed in Phase 06 or to `screen.id`.
findings.why: The fix listed for L9 ('the URL must equal the screen htmlCode.downloadUrl') was applied, but that only ties the two fields inside the same untrusted answer together: an answer that names any path on the right host as both its `screen.htmlCode.downloadUrl` and its `htmlUrl` passes. The permission is bound to the host and to a second field in the same answer, not to the resource that is fetched; the L9 twin 'the licence checked on one input and the fetch made on another' still holds for the path.
findings.fix: Require the URL's path to match the download prefix observed in the Phase 06 receipt, or require the screen `id` returned in the same answer to appear in the URL path, before `download()` is allowed to fetch it.
findings.twin_of: Paths compared without percent-encoding normalisation -> normalise both sides of a path comparison the same way

findings.breaking_input: An HTML draft whose `srcset` candidate list contains two URLs that overlap in offset after `decodeAttr` runs (e.g. `srcset="https://cdn.tailwindcss.com/a.png 1x, https://cdn.tailwindcss.com/aa.png 2x"`), so the offsets computed from `a.value.matchAll(...)` are applied to the original attribute text while the edits for the parent tag's other attributes were computed against the same value. `applyEdits` sorts by `start` and refuses overlaps (`if (sorted[i].end > sorted[i-1].start) throw new Error("two rewrites overlap")`), and `vendor()` catches that throw only around the HTML pass — so `applyEdits(html, edits)` throwing here returns `{unresolved: ["two rewrites overlap"]}`, which is the correct refusal. But the stylesheet pass (`css` body) calls `applyEdits(css, edits)` inside `fetchOne` with no try/catch, so an overlap in a stylesheet escapes to the top-level catch and becomes 'internal error' with a class name — the same one-status-line contract holds, but the stylesheet's actual reason (a conflict the reader can name) is replaced by an internal error code, and the draft is retried against the provider with a different outcome class.
findings.why: The B2 fix rewrote by offsets and refuses overlaps in `applyEdits`, but the stylesheet caller does not convert the overlap into a named unresolved reason the way the HTML caller does. The fix for the twin 'a rewrite by global split/join' left the stylesheet path to a generic internal error, so the failure is not namable in `status.log` the way the HTML path's is; the receipt records an internal error code a later reader cannot distinguish from a real crash.
findings.fix: Wrap the stylesheet `applyEdits(css, edits)` in a try/catch that pushes the reason into `unresolved` (like the HTML path), or have `applyEdits` return a structured overlap result.
findings.twin_of: A parser throw left to a stack trace beside two guarded siblings -> every step that can fail answers with a named ERR line

findings.breaking_input: `docs/design/explore/jx/rival-stitch/../../variant-a/index.html` passed as the render route. The route case `docs/design/explore/*/rival-*/?*` — `*` in a POSIX case pattern crosses `/` — matches with the first `*` taking `jx`, `rival-*` taking `rival-stitch/../..`, and `?*` taking `variant-a/index.html`. The per-part split later takes `${ROUTE#docs/design/explore/}` and looks for the second `/`; if the explore id is the segment up to the first `/`, `_er_variant` is then `rival-stitch/../..`, which does NOT match `rival-*`'s nested refusal (that branch tests `${_er_variant#rival-}` and finds `stitch/../..`, which contains `/` — the nested case's `*[!a-z0-9-]*` pattern refuses because of the `/`, so the refusal fires, but only *because* `/` is outside the alphabet; a route like `rival-stitchX/../variant-a` would leave `_er_variant=rival-stitchX/..`).
findings.why: The L14 fix claim was 'tighten the route to a plain alphabet', but the rival route branch was added before the per-part split and it still uses a `*` that crosses `/`; the only defence is that the later nested case happens to reject `/`. If a route is shaped so the dividing slash falls after a rival-* segment without an interior `/` (e.g. `docs/design/explore/x/rival-zz/../variant-a/index.html` where the split point is at a different place), the page rendered can be outside the rival dir. The check on `EXPLORE_PAGE` (`*//*|*/./*|*/../*`) is textual, and the pattern language can expand `/../` through the earlier crossing `*`.
findings.fix: Before the case, require the route to have exactly the expected number of `/` separators, reject any segment equal to `.`, `..` or empty, and test `_er_variant` against a plain alphabet (`[a-z0-9-]`) rather than a negation class.
findings.twin_of: A textual `..` check on a pattern language that can expand -> hold an expanding pattern to a plain alphabet instead of searching it for bad substrings

findings.breaking_input: The test `jury: a rival is dealt blind` asserts `r[0].provenance === "rival:stitch@0.3.5"`. The code constructs `provenance: `rival:${p}@${ver[2]}`` where `ver[2]` is the version half of `@google/stitch-sdk@0.3.5` — i.e. `0.3.5`. So the test and code agree on the single-`@` shape, which is the fix. But `tests/design-jury.bats:392` in the prior finding L15 asserted `"rival:stitch@@google/stitch-sdk@0.3.5"`. The test file now asserts the fixed string, and the fix was applied — but the `_rival_fixture` helper writes a receipt with `"sdk":"@google/stitch-sdk@0.3.5"` (no leading space issues), and a future `rec.sdk` written without the `@` scope (e.g. `"stitch-sdk@0.3.5"`) would still match `ver` and produce `rival:stitch@0.3.5`. The test does not cover the case where `rec.sdk` names a different package; a test that only checks the string for the one fixture enshrines the fixture's package, not the rule.
findings.why: The L15 fix was 'parse pkg@version, refuse without one, stamp rival:provider@version'. The version regex does not check the package NAME — only the prefix `@?[a-z0-9][a-z0-9._/-]*`. A receipt with `"sdk":"@evil/sdk@9.9.9"` passes and the key carries `rival:stitch@9.9.9`, which is a stamp naming a package the Stitch adapter never used. The test asserts the exact string for the fixture and so does not detect the missing package binding.
findings.fix: Compare the parsed package name to `PROVIDERS[pname].pkg`'s name and version, and refuse a receipt whose package is not the pinned one; the test should assert the refusal for `"sdk":"@evil/sdk@9.9.9"`.
findings.twin_of: A registry lint accepted an id its consumer refuses -> the lint enforces the consumer's own grammar, so a row that lints is a row that can be used

findings.breaking_input: An explore whose `explore.txt` has a line `brief=docs/design/briefs/lexos/brief.md extra` — the code strips the prefix `docs/design/briefs/`, then strips the suffix `/brief.md`, leaving `lexos/brief.md extra`; the case `*/*` refuses because of the interior `/`. But `brief=docs/design/briefs//brief.md` leaves `BRIEF_ID=` empty and is refused. A line `brief=docs/design/briefs/CON/brief.md` leaves `CON` (uppercase) and is refused by the character class. The hole: `brief=docs/design/briefs/lexos-../lexos/brief.md` — the prefix strip yields `lexos-../lexos/brief.md`, then the suffix strip removes the trailing `/brief.md` leaving `lexos-../lexos` — the interior `/` refuses. A line with a trailing carriage return (`brief=docs/design/briefs/lexos/brief.md\r`) — `BRIEF_ID` after the two strips is `lexos/brief.md\r`, refused because of `/`. The reachable hole: `brief=docs/design/briefs/lexos/brief.md` on a file with CRLF — `BRIEF_ID` is `lexos\r`, and the character class `*[!a-z0-9-]*` refuses because `\r` is outside. So the shell already refuses CRLF by accident, but the error message says 'names no brief under docs/design/briefs/<id>/brief.md' and hides a CRLF track from a checkout — the twin of the record parser CRLF pattern.
findings.why: The code strips the suffix `/brief.md` literally and then refuses a CR — the diagnostic is wrong and the fix for the CRLF record pattern ('strip CR before anchoring any line of a tracked text file') was applied to other readers but not here. A brief on a CRLF checkout is not parsed; the error names a missing brief rather than a carriage return.
findings.fix: Strip a trailing `\r` from `BRIEF_LINE` before any suffix strip, as other records do, and keep the same refusal for other characters.
findings.twin_of: A record parsed with an end anchor on a CRLF checkout -> strip CR before anchoring any line of a tracked text file

findings.breaking_input: The receipt JSON written by `settle` is `scrub(JSON.stringify(receipt, null, 2)) + "\n"`. When `key` is null (the 'no key' path) `scrub` returns its argument unchanged. When the SDK error message contains a substring that is a regular expression metacharacter in the key — `String(t).split(key)` splits on the LITERAL key string, not the regex, so that is safe. The hole: the receipt records `receipt.error.code = field(err.code)` but `scrub` is applied to the whole JSON string, so a key that appears inside the JSON's own escaped form (e.g. a `"` in the key becomes `\"` in JSON and the literal-key split no longer matches) survives the scrub. A key like `abc"def` written into the JSON as `abc\"def` is not caught by `split(key)` on the serialized form, and the receipt carries the key in its JSON-escaped spelling.
findings.why: The B11 fix routed throws to `fail()`, and the scrub is applied to the JSON string. The scrub matches the raw key against the serialized form, so any key character that JSON escapes (double quote, backslash, control characters, `/`) is present in the file in its escaped spelling and is not scrubbed — the same class as the fixed 'scrub that matched after sanitising, or before it', but applied to the serialized record.
findings.fix: Scrub the receipt's individual string fields before serialization (each field through `String(x).split(key).join("<key>")`), and serialize an object whose strings were already scrubbed; or scrub the JSON with a regex-escaped key against both raw and JSON-escaped spellings.
findings.twin_of: A scrub that matched after sanitising, or before it -> delete control characters, then scrub, then print through one printer

findings.breaking_input: The `key` object written to `join(ex.jury, "key.json")` is `JSON.stringify(key, null, 2)`. The rival's `provenance` from `rec.sdk` is written verbatim into the key — it comes from a JSON file the jury did not author. `String(rec.sdk)` can include a newline, a `\r`, or a Unicode line separator; the regex `^(@?[a-z0-9][a-z0-9._/-]*)@([0-9][0-9A-Za-z.+-]{0,40})$` does not admit those, so the version half is constrained. But `rec.sdk` is only checked by regex; when the version is `ver[2]`, the provenance is `rival:${p}@${ver[2]}` — both halves are constrained by the pname grammar and the version regex, so the key field is clean. The hole is the DEAL line: `console.log(clean(`design-explore jury: rival ${p} LEFT OUT -- ${last ? last.split("\t").slice(2).join(" ") : "..."}; ...`))` — `last` is read from `status.log` with `readFileSync` and split on `\r?\n`, then filtered on `l.split("\t")[1] === p`. The `status.log` is written by the adapter with `field(scrub(detail))` which strips control characters. But the adapter's `field` regex is `/[\u0000-\u001f\u007f\u0085\u2028\u2029]+/g` — it does not strip `\u2028`? It does (`\u2028\u2029` are in the class). So a `status.log` field from another tool (not the adapter) can carry `\u0085` and the jury prints it; `clean` is the jury's own printer and the L10 fix says 'strip every line-breaking code point, not only C0 and DEL' — if `clean` strips all those, fine, but if `clean` is the older printer the unicode separator reaches the terminal.
findings.why: The reviewer's 'Unicode line separators passed a control-character scrub' pattern was listed as a fixed-defect elsewhere but this diff adds a new reader of `status.log` (the rival LEFT OUT line) and a new printer of its contents; the fix to one scrub is not checked in the new reader. A `status.log` written by a sibling tool with a different scrubber can inject a line separator into the deal's stderr/stdout.
findings.fix: Run `last`'s detail through the same `field`/`clean` as the adapter, and assert at test time that a `status.log` with `\u2028` in the third column is printed as one line.
findings.twin_of: A fixed scrub with an unfixed twin in the next file -> every writer of remote or registry text into a line scrubs it; grep the pattern, not the file

findings.breaking_input: A rival with a DRAFTED receipt whose `sdk` is a package whose version half is `0.3.5.0` or `0.3.5-rc1` — accepted by the regex. The provenance is `rival:stitch@0.3.5-rc1`. Phase 08's packager (not in this diff) parses the stamp at the first `@` — since `ver[1]` may include `/` (`@arc/stitch@0.1.0`), the package name is `@arc/stitch` and the version `0.1.0`, and the stamp written is `rival:stitch@0.1.0`. The package used to draft is lost: the deal stamps the version but not the package name, so a Phase 08 read cannot tell that the package was `@arc/stitch`. The pinned package for `stitch` is `@google/stitch-sdk`; a receipt naming `@arc/stitch` produces a stamp that reads as if Stitch's own SDK at a different version.
findings.why: The fix for L15 ('parse pkg@version, stamp rival:provider@version') deliberately dropped the package name from the stamp. But the sealed prediction is about a SPECIFIC rival (Stitch, ADR-1413), and the packager refuses a rival whose provider is not the cleared one — with only a version in the stamp, the package identity is not in the key. A later reader cannot tell the cleared `@google/stitch-sdk@0.3.5` from an arbitrary `@arc/stitch@0.3.5` receipt. The test asserts `rival:stitch@0.3.5` for the one fixture and so does not exercise this.
findings.fix: Include the package name in the provenance (`rival:<provider>:<pkg>@<version>`) or add a separate `rivalPackage` field to the key item, and require it to equal `PROVIDERS[pname].pkg`.
findings.twin_of: A source of truth moved from one deletable thing to another -> cross-check the two records: every arm pairs.json names (parsed by `design-expa1.mjs arms`) must be a real directory, or refuse

findings.breaking_input: `download()` calls `readCapped(res, MAX_HTML_BYTES)` and `readCapped` throws `{code:"TOO_LARGE"}` when the body exceeds the cap, then `download` catches and re-throws with the same code. A 0-byte 200 (a provider that returns an empty body with `content-length: 0`) passes `res.status === 200` and produces an empty Buffer; `draft` then does `if (body.length === 0) return fail("unusable answer (the HTML is empty)")`. Fine. But `readCapped` reads `res.body ?? []` and a `HEAD`-like empty stream leaves `chunks` empty. The hole in `childTransport` is different: on the `close` event the child's `out` is parsed for the first non-empty line, and `finish` is called; the `backstop` timeout is set, but the `timer` for `DRAFT_DEADLINE_MS` was cleared in `finish` and the `backstop` is only set inside `finish`. If `child.on("close")` fires before `child.stdout` drains, `out` is partial and `JSON.parse` fails, producing a NO_ANSWER rather than the child's real answer — the B10 twin 'judging a stream before it is drained'. The diff says the answer is handed back 'only once the child (and its tree) is gone', but the code calls `finish` on `close`, which is when stdout is closed — the stream has been flushed by then in Node, so this is likely fine in practice, but the backstop race (`backstop = setTimeout(..., 10000)`) can fire and close the answer before the child's group is reaped.
findings.why: The fix for the stream-drain pattern was to end on `close`, and this code does — but the added `backstop` (10s) can resolve the verdict before the kill tree completes, so the caller's `rmSync(runDir)` in `finally` can run while a grandchild still holds the temp dir on Windows (the exact EBUSY case the fix wanted to avoid). The fix names 'kill, wait for close' but the backstop breaks the wait.
findings.fix: Only resolve after both `close` and the kill tree's completion (poll for the group's exit, or wait for `taskkill` to return), and remove the backstop's ability to resolve before the tree is reaped; if the tree is unreapable, record that as its own named outcome.
findings.twin_of: Judging a stream before it is drained -> end on 'close'; kill, wait for close, then judge doubled ids
